idiom_name: for range loop with an accumulator variable; generic Fold[S ~[]E, E, A any] when the operation is reused
implementation_notes: Go ships no fold: the slices package offers Index, Contains, Concat, Collect, Sorted and Chunk but no Fold or Reduce (verified against the upstream source), so the pattern is the loop the language is built around - `for _, v := range xs { acc = f(acc, v) }` with an immutable-by-convention accumulator that the body returns. Since Go 1.18 the reusable form is five lines of generics (Fold over a slice type), worth writing when many call sites share an operation but not worth an abstraction for a single use, because the plain loop inlines and keeps the accumulator in registers. For a recursive data type the fold is a hand-written function over the node struct; early exit is a return from the loop body, which the language expresses directly and cheaply.
pitfalls: Go has no right fold and no tail-call optimization: a recursive fold over a deep tree grows the goroutine stack until the runtime aborts with a fatal stack-exceeds error, so input-driven depth needs an explicit stack or a worklist.
Folding a map iterates in randomized order: any non-commutative combine over map keys returns a different result per run - sort the keys (slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))) or fold over a slice.

A fold that captures an outer variable and mutates it instead of threading the accumulator through the loop is untestable and unusable in a parallel or iterator-based setting; take the accumulator in and return it.

variants.name: Iterator fold over iter.Seq with yield-driven early exit
variants.idiom_name: func Fold[E, A any](seq iter.Seq[E], init A, f func(A, E) A) A over a push iterator
variants.implementation_notes: Go 1.23's range-over-func protocol makes a fold expressible over any sequence rather than over a materialized slice: an iterator is iter.Seq[E] (func(yield func(E) bool), with iter.Seq2 for key/value), a fold is a function that ranges over it, and returning false from the yield function - which is what happens when the range body returns - is the sanctioned early-exit channel for streaming and lazily produced sources. iter.Pull converts a push iterator into next/stop functions when an explicit pull loop is needed, and the slices/maps packages supply the adapters (slices.Values, maps.Keys, slices.Collect) that connect built-in containers to the protocol. Choose the iterator form when the source is generated (a walk, a query, a stream) or when the fold must stop early; keep the plain range loop for slices, where it allocates nothing.
pitfalls: Cleanup belongs to the producer: a fold that exits early relies on the range statement (or iter.Pull's stop function) to let the producer run its deferred cleanup, so abandoning a pull iterator without calling stop leaks whatever the producer set up.
Iterator folds allocate a closure per call and defeat inlining in hot loops; for slices of known size the direct range loop over the slice is measurably faster and clearer.
An iter.Seq built from a map still yields randomized order, and an unbounded iterator (a generator that never returns false) hangs a fold exactly as it would hang a loop.
